chapters.title: The Elements of Behavior
chapters.keys: Stop blaming yourself and look at behavior as a design problem with three parts. His Behavior Model says a behavior happens when Motivation (the desire to do it), Ability (the capacity to do it) and a Prompt (the cue that says do it now) come together at the same moment; he shortens this to B=MAP. The Action Line is the curve on his model's chart: when motivation and ability put a behavior above it, a prompt makes it happen; below it, the behavior does not happen when prompted. Motivation and ability trade off, so the harder a behavior is, the more motivation it needs, and the easier it is, the less it needs. Without a prompt, no behavior happens, however motivated or able you are. When a behavior is not happening, check in his order: first the prompt, then ability, and only then motivation. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Katie, a successful executive, kept scrolling social media on her phone in bed after her early alarm instead of getting up; she started leaving the phone in the kitchen at night and got an old-fashioned alarm clock for the bedroom, and the scrolling in bed stopped.

chapters.title: Motivation: Focus on Matching
chapters.keys: Do not build change on motivation, because it rises and falls and cannot be counted on. His Motivation Wave is that rise and fall: a big spike of motivation is good for doing a really hard thing once, but it fades, so it cannot carry a habit you must keep up. Separate an Aspiration (an abstract want) and an Outcome (a measurable result) from a Behavior (a specific thing you can do now). His Behavior Design steps run in order: clarify the aspiration, explore behavior options, then match yourself with specific behaviors. A Swarm of Behaviors is a brainstorm of many specific behaviors that could reach the aspiration. Focus Mapping sorts that swarm by how much each behavior would help and whether you can get yourself to do it. You keep the Golden Behaviors, the ones that are effective, that you want to do, and that you can do. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Sandra and Adrian bought their first home and were excited to turn its neglected backyard into a garden; the excitement faded, they felt overwhelmed and did not know where to start, and Fogg says they had put all their eggs in the motivation basket.

chapters.title: Ability: Easy Does It
chapters.keys: Make the behavior easy, because simplicity changes behavior. Ask his Discovery Question, what is making this behavior hard to do, and check it against the Ability Chain, his five links of time, money, physical effort, mental effort and routine, where the weakest link decides how hard the behavior is. He gives three ways to make a behavior easier: raise your skill, get tools and resources, or make the behavior tiny. To make it tiny, use a Starter Step, the first small move toward the full behavior, or Scaling Back, shrinking the behavior to a tiny version of itself. Keep the tiny version small enough that you can do it even on a bad day. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Sarika, a project manager in Bangalore who has bipolar disorder, could not keep up the routines that helped her, so she shrank them to turning on the stove burner first thing in the morning and sitting on her meditation cushion for three breaths; those tiny steps grew into cooking breakfast and a daily meditation practice.

chapters.title: Prompts: The Power of After
chapters.keys: Give every new habit a clear prompt. He names three kinds: a Person Prompt, something inside you such as a bodily urge or simply remembering, which he calls unreliable; a Context Prompt, a cue in your surroundings such as a note or an alarm; and an Action Prompt, a routine you already do. His best prompt is an Action Prompt used as an Anchor, the existing routine your new habit follows. Write it as a Tiny Habits recipe, After I do my anchor, I will do my new tiny behavior, and follow the ABC order: Anchor, Behavior, Celebration. Pick an anchor that fits the new habit in place, in how often it happens, and in theme, and tie the habit to the trailing edge of the anchor, the very last action of that routine. Pearl Habits use an annoyance as the prompt, and Meanwhile Habits fit a tiny habit into a short wait, such as the seconds while the shower water warms up. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Amy dropped her daughter off at kindergarten every morning, and the car door shutting became her prompt to write her most important task for the day on a Post-it; she stuck it on the dashboard and said Done, and after about a week the habit felt nearly automatic. Fogg's own recipe is two push-ups after he uses the bathroom.

chapters.title: Emotions Create Habits
chapters.keys: Feel good right after you do the behavior, because he says emotions create habits, not repetition. His Celebration is anything you do to make yourself feel positive at once, such as a fist pump or a word of praise to yourself. Shine is his name for the feeling of success a celebration creates. Celebrate immediately after the behavior, because timing matters; he also says you can celebrate when you remember to do the habit and while you are doing it. Find celebrations that feel real to you and practice them until they come naturally. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Fogg himself, during a bad stretch of his life, flossed one tooth one morning, smiled at himself in the mirror and said Victory; he felt his mood lift, did the same on the following days, and the flossing habit took hold, which led him to the idea that emotions create habits.

chapters.title: Growing Your Habits from Tiny to Transformative
chapters.keys: Start tiny and let the habit grow on its own; do not force it bigger. He says habits grow in two ways: a habit grows larger, and habits multiply into more habits. Once the tiny version is rooted, do more when you feel like it, but keep the tiny version as the minimum that still counts on hard days. He says change is a skill you practice, and that small, frequent successes build the confidence and momentum that let change spread. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Sukumar, who had struggled with his weight for years, started with two push-ups after brushing his teeth and a plank of a few seconds; he let them grow at his own pace until he was doing fifty push-ups and a five-minute plank inside a daily one-hour workout.

chapters.title: Untangling Bad Habits: A Systematic Solution
chapters.keys: Treat a bad habit like a knot: loosen the easiest strands first, not the hardest. His Behavior Change Masterplan runs in three phases: first create good new habits, then stop the old habit, then swap it for a new one. Name the bad habit as specific behaviors, and work on one small, specific behavior at a time. To stop one, redesign the prompt first by removing it, avoiding it or ignoring it, then make the behavior harder to do, and only then reduce the motivation. If stopping outright fails, scale back the change (stop for a shorter period, or do the habit for a shorter time or fewer times); if that fails too, swap: keep the prompt and put a new behavior you want and can easily do in place of the old one. Reversal: he says serious addictions call for professional help and are outside this method. Story the author tells: Juni, a radio host, leaned on sugar after her mother died of complications of diabetes; she first built new habits for handling her grief, then listed her specific sugar habits and stopped them one at a time, starting with the easiest, until she had stopped eating sugar.

chapters.title: How We Change Together
chapters.keys: Use the same method to help family, coworkers and teams change, not pressure or guilt. Lead others through the same steps, openly as a Ringleader or quietly as a Ninja. He leans on his two maxims: help people do what they already want to do, and help them feel successful. Ask what is making the behavior hard for them, and make it easier rather than pushing their motivation. Keep the changes tiny and celebrate them with the other person. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Mike wanted his 21-year-old son Chris, who lived at home, to clean the coffee maker's filter, and pushing him brought only resentment; Mike asked for one tiny step at a time (take the filter out, rinse it, put it back) and thanked him for each, and Chris ended up doing it without being asked.
